info.bio:
Hay por lo menos dos artistas con este nombre. Una banda norteamericana de post-hardcore y otra banda indie rock inglesa de britpop.

1) Banda formada por Ian MacKaye (vocalista), Mark Hampton (guitarra), Chris Bald (bajo) e Ivor Hanson (batería) en 1985 en Washington D.C., Estados Unidos. Se separaron un año después.

2) Embrace procede de la zona de Brighouse, al norte de Inglaterra; hasta la fecha han lanzado 5 álbumes, un álbum de singles y un recopilatorio de caras-B.

scenes.desc: Como tantas veces, el fenómeno más publicitado es el menos interesante: un «brit-pop» de grupos terriblemente parecidos y tediosos, sin apenas imaginación. Lo anticipan Lightning Seeds, La's, Teenage Fanclub y Heavenly; estalla con Boo Radleys, Blur (Parklife) y Oasis (el «farol» que mejor personifica la moda). Suede y el glam-pop (Super Furry Animals, Placebo), las excepciones de High Llamas (Hawaii) y Supergrass, el revival mod (Ocean Colour Scene, Wildhearts), Elastica, Sleeper, las Spice Girls; Trembling Blue Stars, Tindersticks, Delgados. El post-pop de Radiohead, «la banda más publicitada y sobrevalorada de la década», cuyo OK Computer es una obra maestra del falso vanguardismo; Coldplay, Travis.

podcast.title: Breakup and Formation of Fugazi
podcast.body: The band eventually broke up, after which Ian MacKaye, a key member, went on to form Fugazi, a group noted for its focus on raw emotion. "Then Embrace broke up, Ian McKay went on to form Fugazi, a band that was all about raw emotion."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Musical Style and Equipment
podcast.body: Embrace's musical style featured loud guitars, prioritizing strumming over complex riffing. Their preferred equipment included Gips, Les Paul, or SG guitars, which were played through Marshall Tube amps, with a strict rule against using transistor amplifiers. "The guitars were loud, but there was less riffing and more strumming. Favorite guitars were Gips and Les Paul's or SG's, played through Marshall Tube amps. No transistors allowed."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Revolution Summer Participation
podcast.body: Embrace was a part of what is remembered as the "Revolution Summer" in the mid-1980s, a period when D.C. hardcore bands aimed to break free from the limiting dogma of traditional hardcore. "They became part of what is now remembered as the Revolution Summer when DC hardcore bands tried to break out of the dogma that had limited what hardcore could be."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Canada's Early Embrace (1963-1964)
xref.body: The Beatles were embraced in Canada nearly a year before their breakthrough in the United States, with songs like "All My Love," "Roll Over Bay, Tovon," and "Twist and Shout" exclusively available there. Capitol Records Canada played a crucial role by manufacturing these records north of the 49th parallel and then exporting at least 100,000, and potentially up to 350,000, copies of each song to the US. "Although the United States gets a lot of attention because it's where the Beatles made their TV debut, it was in Canada where they were embraced first."

xref.title: Pivotal B-52s Moment (1980)
xref.body: At age 11, on January 26, 1980, while watching Saturday Night Live with his older sister Lisa, he witnessed The B-52s perform "Rock Lobster." This performance profoundly impacted him, changing his life and inspiring him to embrace "weirdness" in music. "I remember that moment like some people remember the Kennedy assassination. That moment changed my life."

xref.title: Cassette Club for Distribution (1982)
xref.body: From 1982 onwards, R. Stevie Moore founded his "R. Stevie Moore cassette club" as a primary method for distributing his music. Members of the club would receive a list of his available material, with each song meticulously annotated with a "listenability quotient" that scored precisely how low-fi the recording actually was, reflecting a deliberate embrace and categorization of the lo-fi aesthetic. "Members would get a list of his material with each song annotated with a list-neability quotient, which scored exactly how low-fi the recording really was."

xref.title: Early Days (1991)
xref.body: During the filming of *Singles* in early 1991, Alice in Chains was still in its early stages, primarily "trying to be a glimy hair metal band." This indicates their musical evolution was ongoing and predated their full embrace of the grunge sound that would later define them and the Seattle scene. "Allison James was still trying to be a glimy hair metal band."

xref.title: Career Reassessment after SNL (1992)
xref.body: Sinead viewed the *Saturday Night Live* incident not as a derailment, but as a corrective course for her career. She believed having a number one record had "derailed" her, and tearing the photo put her "on the right track," allowing her to embrace her role as a protest singer and perform live without the pressures of pop stardom or compromise. "I feel that having a number one record derailed my career, and my tearing of the photo put me on the right track."

xref.title: Warped Tour Re-energization (2000)
xref.body: Despite initially refusing ("never, ever play the Warped Tour"), Green Day agreed to join the 2000 Warped Tour after organizer Kevin Lyman offered them a chance to play "with no pressure," hang out with new bands, absorb their energy, and embrace their role as elder statesmen. Playing the tour re-energized the band, introduced them to a new generation of fans, and was pivotal to their career's "second act." "Look, said organizer Kevin Lehmann, here's a chance for you to play some shows with no pressure, hang with the new bands, absorb some of their energy, maybe bask in your role as the elder statesman of this community."

xref.title: Accidental Bass Distortion on "Rocket 88"
xref.body: During the recording session for "Rocket 88" on March 2nd, 1951, bass player Willie Kizart's amplifier was accidentally dropped, jarring loose the speaker cone. This resulted in a distinctive buzz and vibration. Producer Sam Phillips decided to embrace this "cool" distorted sound, which became a new and defining characteristic of the track, potentially making it the first rock and roll record. "But then producer Sam Phillips, a white guy, said, hold on, sounds kind of cool. Let's use it as is."

xref.title: Advocacy for Women in Rock
xref.body: Ellie Rowsell is a vocal advocate for increasing female representation in rock and roll, stating that "There are many aspects of life that need more women in them and rock and roll is certainly one." She actively encourages more women to embrace being rock stars. "This woman not only loves to rock out, but she also wants to share the experience. ... She wants more women to dare to be rock stars. Here's a quote from Ellie. There are many aspects of life that need more women in them and rock and roll is certainly one."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Akai S1000's Impact on Debut Album
xref.body: Trent Reznor, then an employee at a Cleveland Music Store, was among the first to fully embrace the capabilities of the Akai S1000 sampler. This instrument was so integral to the sound of Nine Inch Nails that the band's first album would not have achieved its distinctive sound without it. "And without the S1000, the first 9-inch nails album could have not ever sounded like this."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Alternative Radio Play
xref.body: For a period, it was common to hear Depeche Mode played on alternative radio stations alongside early hip hop acts like Run DMC or Rakim, indicating an initial embrace of rap by some parts of the alternative scene. "it wasn't unusual to hear run DMC or rareg being rekeemed played next to Dopech mode on alternative radio stations."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Biggest New Romantic Band
xref.body: Duran Duran is recognized as the biggest band to emerge from the New Romantic subculture. This movement, characterized by its flamboyant fashion and embrace of synthesizers, saw the band rise to prominence with its distinctive sound and visual style. "Durand Durand, the biggest of the bands to emerge out of the subculture known as the New Romantics."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Contemporary Sound
xref.body: Anberlin is presented as an example of a Tooth and Nail band whose sound, as demonstrated by "Embrace the Dead," is far from traditional religious music. "That ain't grandma's religious music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Dave Gahan's Embrace of Rock God Persona
xref.body: During the "Songs of Faith and Devotion" tour, Dave Gahan fully adopted a "rock god" image, which was visibly expressed through changes in his hairstyle and the acquisition of additional tattoos. One notable tattoo on his shoulder blades required a painful ten-hour session to complete. "Dave had totally embraced the rock god thing by this point. We saw changes in hairstyle, more tattoos, including one on his shoulder blades that took 10 painful hours."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: David Bowie Fan
xref.body: Johnson was a huge fan of David Bowie, an influence that likely played a role in his own theatrical stage presence and embrace of provocative imagery. "He was also a huge David Bowie fan."

xref.title: Deepening into Alt-Rock
xref.body: As listeners immersed themselves further into the 1990s alternative music scene, they would often discover bands like Jane's Addiction, signifying an embrace of diverse and influential acts from the era.

xref.title: Defying Music Industry Fears
xref.body: At a time when the music industry was "freaking out" over file sharing, the Arctic Monkeys leveraged it to become famous. Despite industry warnings that giving away music for free would lead to financial ruin, the band continued to embrace online sharing. This approach proved that sharing music online could broaden and deepen a band's appeal, setting a new standard for rapidly building a passionate fanbase.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early Big Muff Adopter
xref.body: Jimi Hendrix was one of the first musicians to purchase and embrace the Big Muff pedal. He acquired his first unit at Many's Music Store in New York City and immediately recognized its potential, subsequently using it on one of his songs where both distortion and controlled feedback are prominent. "One of the first people to buy one was Jimmy Hendrix, who walked into many's music store in New York City and loved what he could do with it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Distortion and Feedback

xref.title: Early Home Recording Pioneer (1950s-1970s)
xref.body: Coming from a musical background, with his father Bob Moore playing on recordings for Elvis and Roy Orbison, R. Stevie Moore was inspired to make his own recordings at home. He utilized whatever gear he could assemble with his dad, including cheap cassette recorders or secondhand reel-to-reel machines, and began releasing records through his own label by the late 1950s. His work demonstrated an early embrace of home recording as a means of artistic expression. "R. Steve Moore was also in love with the cassette. The idea of being able to quickly record something on his reel to reel machine and then dub off copies onto cassettes for distribution was very appealing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Embrace Vocalist
xref.body: Guy Picciotto, formerly the singer for Rites of Spring, also featured as a member of the proto-emo group Embrace. "Embrace also featured Rites of Spring singer Guy Piccoedo."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Embrace by Gen X Alt-Rockers
xref.body: Björk's 1993 solo album, "Debut," was released during the height of the Grunge explosion. Her innovative sound and experimental nature resonated deeply with the alt-rock nation of Gen Xers, who were open to new ideas and embraced her, leading her to introduce them to diverse musical styles. "many of the alt-rock nation of Gen Xers were very open to new ideas, they embraced Bjork and she, in turn, taught them something about different musical styles from tripop to cell stuff that was more Yorkish."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Embrace of "Hollow Notes" Sound
xref.body: During the production of "Michigan Left," the band underwent a "turning point" where they became open to more influences, particularly synth sounds referred to as "Hollow notes." Previously, they "hated Hollow notes" and focused on a guitar-driven, edgy sound for "Jackson Square," but on "Michigan Left," they found these nuanced synth sounds "actually kind of sound interesting," leading to a slightly more nuanced record. "I hated Hollow notes before we made Michigan left. And then I was sort of, those synths actually kind of sound interesting."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Arkells - In Their Own Words:  Part 2

xref.title: Embrace of Individuality in Punk
xref.body: The Talking Heads thrived in the late 1970s punk rock scene, which allowed artists to express themselves regardless of their identity or musical ability, as long as they had something meaningful to say. This environment was perfect for their unique, nerdy music. "He's a great example of how punk allowed everyone to be who they were. As long as you had something to say, you should be able to say it regardless of who you were or your musical ability."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Embrace of Reggae
xref.body: Ari Up developed a taste for reggae in 1977, which was a radical choice at the time, but reggae's influence was growing due to Jamaican immigration to Britain, fostering a mixing of cultures and music. "Ari developed a taste for reggae. And this is more radical than it sounds right now. See today, reggae and scott, that's everywhere, right? Not so in 1977, but that was changing thanks to the political and economic situation in Jamaica."

xref.title: Evolution into Glitter Rock
xref.body: Iggy Pop's career evolved to embrace elements of glitter rock, finding a home for the second wave of glam in America. "the evolution of the careers of Lou Reed and Iggy Pop."

xref.title: Evolution into Glitter Rock
xref.body: Lou Reed's career evolved to embrace elements of glitter rock, finding a home for the second wave of glam in America. "the evolution of the careers of Lou Reed."

xref.title: Fascination and Adoption of Synthesizers
xref.body: David Bowie was deeply fascinated by the electronic music Kraftwerk was creating and quickly immersed himself in using synthesizers. His embrace of this technology captured public attention and contributed to the wider acceptance of electronic sounds in popular music. "David Bowie was fascinated by what craft work was doing and immediately dove into synthesizers and that got people's attention."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Feminization of Male Rock Stars
xref.body: Bowie was the first to openly and unabashedly feminize the macho male rock and roll star. His pioneering embrace of androgyny led to a subsequent wave of acts that were androgynous, bisexual, gay, or "plain femme looking," including artists like Depeche Mode, Gary Numan, Soft Cell, and Eurythmics. "Bowie was the first to unabashedly and openly feminize the macho male rock and roll star."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: First Wave of Cassette Releases
xref.body: Nina Simone's music was included in the first releases of pre-recorded cassettes in 1965. This made her one of the early artists to be available on the compact cassette format as record labels began to embrace the new technology. "Pre-recorded cassettes started appearing in 1965 with releases from Johnny Mathes, Earth of the Kits and Nina Simone."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Formation of Fugazi
xref.body: After Embrace broke up, Ian MacKaye went on to form Fugazi, a band characterized by its focus on raw emotion and strong ethical principles. "Then Embrace broke up, Ian McKay went on to form Fugazi, a band that was all about raw emotion."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Glam Rock Flamboyance
xref.body: Queen's embrace of glam rock was evident through Freddie Mercury's distinct flamboyance, a direct reflection of the genre's theatricality. "Freddie Mercury's Flamboyance with Queen, glam rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock

xref.title: Guitar Inspiration from Dan
xref.body: While working a summer job at Sounds Interchange in the dub room, Ian befriended Dan, a talented guitar player. Dan played Zappa riffs and songs like Led Zeppelin's "Stairway to Heaven," which deeply impressed Ian and ignited his passion for the guitar. This experience made him realize he could recreate the music he loved with accuracy, leading him to fully embrace the instrument. "once I figured out that correlation of how it came pretty quickly, came pretty easily, but I think the real bug was being able to recreate things that I'd heard and things that I loved."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ian Thornley - In His Own Words: Part 1

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Impact of Bowie's "Coming Out"
xref.body: Boy George of Culture Club openly stated that his life was profoundly changed by David Bowie's public comments in January 1972 about being gay. Bowie's statement gave him the courage to embrace and be true to his own identity. "Boy George of Culture Club and Holly Johnson of Frankie Ghost of Hollywood say that their lives were changed by Bowie's comments."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influence of German Identity
xref.body: Growing up in post-World War II Germany, with a complex and "confused sense of identity" exacerbated by the denazification period, young musicians like Kraftwerk aimed to forge a new musical identity. Their goal was to create music not beholden to American or UK influences, leading them to embrace the modern electronic music of their homeland, often abandoning traditional rock instrumentation. "Their goal came to be the creation of a new form of music that wasn't beholden to what was happening in America or the UK."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influence on Bowie and Punk
xref.body: Described by Bowie as his "crazy new friend," Iggy Pop was a significant inspiration for Bowie's embrace of glam rock. Bowie's friendship with Iggy Pop also contributed to Bowie's "cool" image among the first generation of British punks. "Inspired by Bowlin, his crazy new friend Iggy Pop."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influence on Experimentation
xref.body: Captain Beefheart's ability to create and release such an experimental and unconventional record as *Trout Mask Replica* served as a significant inspiration for other artists, encouraging them to embrace experimentation and difference in their own music. "If he could make a record, others thought, well then so could I."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Initial Band Name and Genre Shift
xref.body: Bad Brains originally started as a jazz fusion group named "Mind Power." As they continued to play, their music became progressively faster and harder, leading them to change their name, inspired by the Ramones' song "Bad Brain," and embrace hardcore. "They started as a jazz fusion group known as Mindpower, but the more they played, the faster and harder the music got. And that's when they changed their name, inspired by the Ramonesong, Bad Brain."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: LGBTQ+ Community Connection
xref.body: Her early gigs, arranged by her minister father, were in gay lounges and clubs, leading to her embrace by the gay community. This loyalty has been reciprocal ever since. "Her first gigs, arranged by her minister father, Belidere Nott, were in gay lounges and clubs. She was embraced by the gay community, and the loyalty has gone both ways ever since."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Driven By Her: Women Who Rocked The 90's

xref.title: Medication Side Effects and Personal Impact
xref.body: The medication Ian Curtis was taking for his epilepsy caused wild mood swings. The fear of having a seizure while holding his baby daughter made him hesitant to embrace her, and he was known to suffer at least two severe seizures weekly. "The men, he was on, caused wild mood swings. When his wife gave birth to a baby daughter, Ian was afraid to hold her or less the seizure begin and he actually hurt her. He could be counted on to have at least two giant seizures a week."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Mod Culture Icon
xref.body: The Who were particularly embraced by the Mod culture, a British subculture that emerged in 1958 and was intensely focused on music, fashion, motor scooters, and drugs. They were a key band for this movement's embrace of British R&B. "and especially the Who."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: New York Origin, UK/Europe Acceptance
xref.body: Formed in New York, The Strokes first found acceptance and embrace in the UK and Europe before making a significant impact in their home country. "The Strokes formed in New York but first embraced in the UK and Europe."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock Chapter: 14

xref.title: Openly Gay Performer in New Wave
xref.body: Boy George was one of the performers in the new wave scene who was, in fact, openly gay. His presence contributed to the genre's embrace of diverse sexual expressions and androgynous looks. "Some of these performers, such as Boy George, were in fact gay."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Early Days of LGBTQ Rock

xref.title: Pioneering All-Electronic New Wave
xref.body: OMD was identified as one of the most significant bands of the Technopop era and among the first of the new wave generation to fully embrace all-electronic sounds. Their approach was rooted in a punk rock aesthetic, despite limited traditional musical ability, focusing on creating new sounds with synthesizers. "The perfect example of late 70s technopop from orchestral maneuvers in the dark, they were one of the first of the new wave generation to turn to all electronic sounds."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Pioneering German Electronic Music
xref.body: In the 1960s, West German artists like Kraftwerk sought to develop a unique musical style that diverged from American and British sounds, leading many to embrace electronic sounds. Kraftwerk emerged as the most influential among them, achieving best-selling albums and international chart success that significantly drew attention to electronic music. "But special props must go to craft work. In the 1960s, Germans, or more correctly West Germans, we're looking for a style of music that they could call their own."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Portastudio Recordings (Early 1990s)
xref.body: This band, based in Dayton, Ohio, under the leadership of Robert Pollard, was actively recording their music using a Portastudio unit during the early 1990s. Their embrace of this home recording technology placed them firmly within the burgeoning low-fidelity scene, reflecting a widespread artistic choice to prioritize raw expression over polished production. "Meanwhile, Robert Pollard was out in Dayton, Ohio, working with his band, Guided By Voices, using a port of studio unit."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Predecessor to Embrace
xref.body: Ian MacKaye was a member of this hardcore band before he was inspired to leave and form Embrace, a proto-emo group. "Everyone was inspired to leave his hardcore band called Minor Threat to form a proto-emo group called Embrace."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Profanity and Anarchy
xref.body: The Sex Pistols gained notoriety for shocking "her majesty's kingdom" with their liberal use of profanity and their embrace of anarchy, particularly highlighted by their infamous television appearance. "The sex pistols shocking the hell out of her majesty's kingdom with their profanity and anarchy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Provider of Comfort to Fans
xref.body: The Cure is mentioned as a band that, similar to Depeche Mode and The Smiths, offered something for troubled, sensitive, shy, and alienated music fans to "hang on to" and embrace for comfort. "Like to pesh mode in the cure, the Smiths gave troubled, sensitive, shy and alienated music fans something to hang on to."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Smiths

xref.title: Reveled in Noise
xref.body: Sonic Youth is recognized as an early and significant influence on the shoegaze genre, particularly for their embrace and "reveling in noise." Their experimental approach to sound contributed to the developing aesthetic of layered, loud, and immersive music. "If there was ever a band that reveled in noise, it was them."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 1

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Significant Presence on Early MTV
xref.body: In the nascent days of MTV, when its entire video library consisted of only about 250 videos, a notable 30 of those were by Rod Stewart. This significant representation highlighted his early embrace of the music video format. "When they signed on, their entire library consisted of about 250 videos and 30 of them were by Rod Stewart."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Transition from Hardcore to Proto-Emo
xref.body: Inspired by the evolving D.C. scene, Ian MacKaye left his hardcore band Minor Threat to form Embrace, which is described as a proto-emo group. "Everyone was inspired to leave his hardcore band called Minor Threat to form a proto-emo group called Embrace."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Trent Resner's Embrace of Remixes
xref.body: Trent Resner, the driving force behind Nine Inch Nails, exhibited a profound appreciation for the possibilities of the remix, frequently releasing full albums and EPs dedicated solely to remixed Nine Inch Nails material. His enthusiasm extended to performing remix "surgery" on songs by other artists. "Trent Resner loves the possibilities of the remix. In fact he was so into it that he released albums and EPs full of remix 9-inch nails material."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Use of Devil's Triad in Jazz (1950s)
xref.body: Charlie Parker, a pioneering figure in jazz, is identified as one of the players who extensively used the "devil's tri tone" (flattened fifth) in his music, particularly during the 1950s. This highlights jazz's embrace of dissonance and complex harmonies for its expressive and innovative qualities. "When jazz came along, these chords were used a lot, especially when we get to the 1950s with players like Charlie Parker and John Coltray."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
